80548490.title: Morris Park Aerodrome
80548490.extract:
The Morris Park Aerodrome was a short-lived airfield in what is now the Morris Park section of the Bronx, New York, United States. The aerodrome, which was in operation from 1908 to 1909, was the first flying field in the United States, occupying the grounds of the former Morris Park Racecourse.  The newly formed Aeronautical Society of New York leased the land in 1908 and used it as an aerodrome for two years until it was developed for residential use.
The Society used the grounds for building and testing aircraft, and for putting on public exhibitions including two major events in November 1908, and June 1909.  The highlight of the former was several glider flights by sixteen-year-old Laurence Lesh, culminating in a crash in which he was severely injured.  The latter had flights by Glenn Curtiss in his Golden Flyer motorized biplane, including the first demonstration of a stable flight around a closed course using ailerons for lateral control.  The exhibitions also featured balloons, kites, helicopters, parachute jumps, and ground vehicles driven by propellers known as wind wagons.  
The aerodrome ceased operations at the end of 1909, when the land was given over to residential development.  The Society moved its operations to a larger facility on Long Island, which would eventually become known as Roosevelt Field.  


== Origins ==

In 1905, the Aero Club of America, patterned after the Aero Club of France, was formed as an outshoot of the Automobile Club of America,  Three years later, in response to sentiment that the aero club should be more active, president Cortlandt Field Bishop appointed a Committee of Aviation, chaired by Albert Triaca, to promote more work on aeroplanes.  The Committee, however, was unable to make any progress; Society chronicler Edward T. Tandy later wrote, "they found their efforts smothered by a cold, wet blanket of official objection. When they attempted to persevere, they were promptly stopped. The power that ruled that organization did not believe in aviation ... The doing of anything practical was not to be attempted."
Unsatisfied with the progress being made by the committee, fifty members of the club split off on June 10, 1908, forming the Aeronautical Society of New York.  Initial membership included Lee Burridge, Albert Triaca, Willard Kimball, Roger Whitman, William Hammer, Leo Stevens, Daniel Brine, and Stanley Beach.  Burridge (who would later be President of the Society) spoke of plans to acquire an airfield: "this society is going to stand for something tangible, practical, and it proposes to secure experimental grounds as soon as possible where men who have been working on problems of aeronautics will be enabled to try out their machines".

That summer, the Society looked at several properties from New Jersey to Long Island and ultimately identified the grounds of the old Morris Park Racecourse as the best location. The racecourse had closed in 1904, after which the 372-acre (151 ha) property was used for automobile and motorcycle racing for a few years. It was convenient to the recently opened West Farms Square subway station and a trolley stop, as well as a range of cafes and residences which could be had for inexpensive rents.  Proximity to public transportation was considered essential, making the field accessible to all experimenters, not just the affluent.
The location provided open spaces on a level elevation, several existing buildings which could be repurposed as workshops, and a larger building with a neatly trimmed lawn and flower beds to use as a clubhouse.  The nearby Woodmansten Inn, built in 1902, had a restaurant and sleeping facilities.  An advertisement in the 1908 exhibition program offered dinner with wine for $3.00 (equivalent to $74 in 2024) and Tandy described it as "one of the best and most fashionable hotels of the city".
Morris Park Aerodrome (occasionally called the Morris Park Volery) was made available to members for the first time on the weekend of August 29 and 30, 1908.  A lease was signed on or about August 31, running until December 31, 1909, although it was already known that the land was eventually destined for residential development.  By September, plans were being made for an exhibition where "Freak machines will have a chance to show what they can do as well as the more orthodox types."  Fences adjacent to the track were removed to provide a clear straight path of at least 0.62 miles (1.00 km), and a machine shop was being constructed.


== The field ==

Morris Park was the first flying field in the United States although by the end of 1909, All the World's Air-Ships by Fred Jane listed it as one of eight such facilities in the country.  In addition to being used for flight instruction (being home to the International School of Aeronautics run by Albert Triaca) the primary purpose of the field and the Society was the construction of aircraft.  Within the first 12 months of operation, 24 full-sized heavier-than-air airplanes were constructed on the field, plus an assortment of gliders, airships, and a large number of scale models. Almost 25% of the Society membership held aircraft patents or were directly involved in the construction of aircraft at the field.
Lacking any hill high enough to launch a glider from, the Society built two facilities for assisting in glider launches.  The first was a catapult.  The second was a larger structure of wooden construction, which was erected without first obtaining a building permit.  After a glider spent an entire day atop the structure waiting for winds favorable for launching, city officials declared that the structure was a residence, and since it lacked both plumbing and a fire escape, condemned it, compelling it to be torn down.
Many of the aircraft built at Morris Park were failures.  Aviation historian Paul Glenshaw wrote of the Aeronautic Society's efforts:

The group could boast of few successes. Descriptions of the members’ experiments included words like “tree” and “fence,” coupled with “plunged” and “smashed.”


== 1908 exhibition ==
On October 18, the first exhibition of the Society was announced for November 3 to coincide with election day.  There were plans for two airplanes from the Aerial Experiment Association (June Bug and Silver Dart) to compete, a five-mile dirigible race, kites, and gliders; the kite contest was open to public school students with no entry fee. There were also plans for one-, five-, and ten-mile motorcycle races sponsored by the Federation of American Motorcyclists and for the U.S. Weather Bureau to demonstrate the use of kites and captive balloons to collect atmospheric data.  Lillian Todd, the only female member of the Society, was expected to show a "large model airplane" of her own design.
Admission to the exhibition was $0.50 (equivalent to $17.5 in 2024), with the subway ride from Manhattan taking 40 minutes.   An estimated 20,000 spectators showed up, far exceeding expectations. Although several hundred people had volunteered to act as marshals (equipped with badges and sticks), a large number of people swarmed past the gate with only about 3,500 people having paid their admission fee.  Tandy wrote that in the years since the race track had been in use, the fences had deteriorated and that "The payment for admission proved a matter of almost Quixotic courtesy."


=== Laurence Lesh ===

A glider piloted by sixteen-year-old Laurence J. Lesh crashed during its third flight after reaching a maximum altitude of 70 feet (21 m) and travelling a total of about 200 feet (61 m).  One account attributed the cause of the crash to inexperience flying this model of glider which lacked the rudder used on his earlier designs. Another blamed the crowd which got in his way while attempting to land.  In any case, the injuries sustained in the crash sent Lesh to the hospital and he took a year of rehabilitative therapy to fully recover from his broken ankle.
The glider had been launched by rope tow behind a 1907 Thomas Flyer driven by Montague Roberts, one of the drivers who had won the 1908 New York to Paris Race in that car. Montague had also competed in a 1907 24-hour race held at Morris Park when it was previously used for automobile racing.  Previous launch attempts that day had used a tow horse; out of six tries, only two got off the ground, reaching an altitude of about 20 feet (6.1 m).
Lesh had also planned to show a large box kite that day.  Lesh, a protégé of Octave Chanute, was a native of Iowa who moved to Montreal as a child.  He was the first known aviator in Canada, having built and flown horse-drawn gliders as early as 1907. Lesh also completed a record-setting 24 minute, 6.2-mile (10.0 km) flight in 1907 towed by a motor boat on the St. Lawrence River.


=== Wind wagon races ===
The exhibition included a wind wagon contest, these being wheeled ground vehicles driven by propeller thrust.  The New York Times described them as resembling "a huge tricycle with a propeller eight feet long in front and a gasoline motor behind".  Inventors scheduled to show their wagons included astronomer William Pickering, aviation pioneer Glenn Curtiss, W. A. Custard, and Julian P. Thomas. According to Curtiss, the purpose of the wind wagon was to test the power of motors and the efficiency of propellers and it had no commercial value.
Thomas's machine was wrecked two days before the exhibition, when he crashed during a practice run while trying to avoid a motorcycle.  About 40 motorcyclists were using the track to prepare for a race scheduled to be held on exhibition day; Thomas believed they had already cleared the track and entered the course, running at high speed.  He sustained severe injuries which were initially thought to have been fatal, but after several minutes of unconsciousness, he opened his eyes, asked for a cigarette, and refused to be taken to a hospital.  Recuperating at home, Thomas asked that the machine be repaired so another driver could use it during the exhibition.


== Retrospective ==
Two weeks after the 1908 exhibition, Lee Burridge spoke at the November 2 annual meeting of the Aero Club, reflecting on the scism which led to the founding of the Aeronautical Society.  He complained of the "apathy of the Aero Club" when, after he had identified Morris Park as a potential site, they failed to act on the opportunity.  Augustus Post, secretary of the Aero Club, replied that doing so would have split the membership into two classes, to which he was opposed.  Post added that the club was still seeking to "secure extensive grounds for motor ballooning and aeroplaning, with hydrogen gas facilities, machine shops, and suitable buildings for storage, within easy distance of the city".
Members of the opposition group who had split off to form the new society acknowledged that while Morris Park was too small, it would serve a temporary function while they continued to search for a larger facility.  A motion authorizing the Aero Club to work together with the Aeronautical Society to jointly search for a location was discussed, but failed.  


== 1909 exhibition ==

A second annual exhibition was held on June 26, 1909, with 2000 people in attendance on a day with ideal flying weather but with near-record high temperatures.  The low attendance left the Society with a $5,000 (equivalent to $120,000 in 2024) deficit.


=== Glenn Curtiss ===
The highlight of the event was a series of flights by Curtiss in a biplane named the Golden Flyer which the Society had purchased from Curtiss and his partner Augustus Herring for $5,000.  This set a number of records; the flights themselves were the first airplane flights ever taken over New York City, the purchase was the first to a civilian owner, and the Herring-Curtiss Company was the first aeroplane manufacturing company in the country.  The terms of the sale included training for two pilots (Charles Willard and Alexander Williams), and an obligation for Curtiss to fly it the exhibition.  The Curtiss design used ailerons for roll control instead of the wing warping system employed by the Wright Brothers, making the airplane more stable and more maneuverable.

The flight of the Golden Flyer created legal controversy when two months later the Wright Brothers filed a patent infringement suit against the Aeronautic Society in the United States Circuit Court, claiming infringement of their 1906 patent.   The suit (one of many the Wrights would eventually file against competitors) demanded that the Society be permanently injuncted from further infringement, disclose how much money had been made from the exhibitions, and turn over for destruction all "machinery, flying machines, and parts thereof" which infringed the patents.
The first flight was a straight-line flight covering 300 yards (270 m), averaging 30 feet (9.1 m) in altitude.  The Brooklyn Eagle noted that "his adjustment of his controls to uneven wind currents was absolutely accurate".  The remainder of the flights took place after twilight, having been delayed by puffy winds, with the event being forced to conclude as darkness fell. The rough ground at the field was a complicating factor, making landings difficult.  One flight lasted 1 minute 45 2/5 seconds, completing a lap around the 1-mile (1.6 km) track at an altitude of 20 feet (6.1 m), flying between trees along the backstretch and sometimes reaching as high as 60 feet (18 m).  The aircraft was reported as "always under perfect control".  This flight was the first time Curtiss had completed a flight around a circular course, although Henri Farman and the Wright Brothers had both already accomplished this feat.  Curtiss had hesitated before making the turn at the north end of the track, which had been criticized as being too confining.


=== William Martin ===

William H. Martin flew a glider towed by an automobile driven by his wife.  He had only gone about 50 yards (46 m) when the tow rope broke and the glider crashed; he suffered minor injuries but the aircraft was severely damaged. The safety of the craft was demonstrated on September 21 when Martin's eight-year-old granddaughter, Blanche, made several solo flights, becoming the youngest person to make a flight in a heavier-than-air craft.
Martin's glider had originally been constructed on his farm in Canton, Ohio, equipped with sled runners for operation on snow.  The V-shaped lower wings added stability as a result of the dihedral effect.  It first flew on January 12, 1909, launched from the top of a hill and towed by Martin's horse named Old Billy.  The first flight covered 200 feet (61 m) reaching a maximum altitude of 25 feet (7.6 m).  Over the next few days, over 100 flights were conducted, with Martin's wife, son, and pet dog all taking turns.  Martin brought the glider to Morris Park in May 1909, where it continued to make demonstration flights, being pulled around the track at 30 miles per hour (48 km/h) behind an automobile with a 150 ft (46 m) tow rope, and reaching altitudes as high as 75 feet (23 m).  By this time, the snow runners had been replaced with wheels.
The UK-based Flight Magazine called the Martin glider demonstration the most notable event of the day, after Curtiss's flight.  They took a negative view, however, of Martin's craft, calling it an "example of the foolhardiness of tests of this character" and writing that "there is little or nothing to be learned through being towed behind a car in this manner ... the conditions do not represent the problems of flight in the least".  They described the flight as a "short and erratic aerial journey".  They noted that the presence of the tow rope restricted operation the aircraft and negatively affected its stability.


=== Additional exhibits ===
Frederick Schneider demonstrated a motor-driven catapult-assisted airplane of his own construction, named The Brooklyn.  The craft failed to get off the ground due to a rusty launching rail and too little weight loaded into the catapult, only managing to slide along the grass for 100 feet (30 m).  There were also parachute jumps from hot air balloons, with Paul Bloomfield jumping from 1,000 feet (300 m), and Mary Hunter from an altitude reported only as "far higher" than Bloomfield's.  One of the less serious events was a "balloonatic race".  This consisted of a person attempting to run while being supported by a lighter-than-air balloon with just enough buoyancy to support the person's weight.


== The Fledglings ==

In attendance at the 1908 exhibition was painter Rudolph Dirks, better known as the cartoonist who drew The Katzenjammer Kids. Based on his experiences at the show, Dirks created an oil-on-linen painting titled The Fledglings. After the show, Dirks quickly returned to his studio in Manhattan where he began work on the painting, working from some rough pencil sketches he had made at the show.  Not having any prepared canvas on hand and wishing to begin work quickly so as not to let his memories of the event fade, Dirks repurposed a linen window shade to use as a canvas.
The painting is considered by aviation historian Tom Crouch to be "the earliest serious artistic reaction to the dawn of the air age".  It was donated by Dirks' son to the National Air and Space Museum where, as of 2025, it is on display in the Early Flight exhibit.


== Other activities ==

The March 1909 issue of Aeronautics included a paper by R. W. Jamieson describing a device used to lay out a screw propeller for an airplane, taking into account the diameter and pitch.  Jamieson described the layout process in a talk to the Society; the device itself was presented to the Society and installed at the Morris Park Aerodrome for use by the society's members.

A report in the April 1909 issue of Aeronautics described new aircraft (referred to as "machines") that were being planned or under construction by at least twenty members of the Society and would be exhibited at Morris Park in the spring of that year. The report noted that Anna Held christened the first aeroplane constructed entirely at Morris Park. The magazine had previously observed that Americans often named their aircraft, contrary to the European habit of numbering them: "Flying machines have a something that is akin to a personality, and giving them names, even if it does not help us to realize their individuality, and perhaps it may, at least it helps in a curiously subtle way to popularize them."  


=== Wilbur Kimball ===
Wilbur R. Kimball's design was a 42-foot (13 m) wingspan biplane with eight four-bladed low-pitch propellers on ball-bearing mounts driven by a 50 horsepower (37 kW) four cylinder two-stroke engine.  Lateral control was achieved by the use of the Neale system: four movable panels set vertically between the two wings. In addition to this airplane, Kimball was also working on another design for William H. Butler which would utilize a 100 horsepower (75 kW) engine.  Kimball's airplane was christened on March 14 by Anna Held as the N. Y. No. 1; the ceremony was believed to be the first time a aeroplane had ever been christened.
On December 4, 1909, a shed containing four of Kimball's aeroplanes was destroyed by fire.  The value of the aeroplanes was estimated at $25,000 (equivalent to $620,000 in 2024).


=== Frederick Schneider ===
In December 1908, a new airplane arrived at Morris Park: a biplane under construction by Frederick Schneider, who had begun construction at his home in Brooklyn, disassembled it there, delivered it to Morris Park on Christmas day, and had it reassembled by the 29th of December. The plane had a 30-foot (9.1 m) wingspan and with a pilot aboard weighed 630 pounds (290 kg) with a main wing loading of 1.7 pounds per square foot (8.3 kg/m2). A 36 horsepower (27 kW) five-cylinder air-cooled engine drove three adjustable-pitch propellers.


=== Stanley Beach and Charles Willard ===

Stanley Beach and Charles Willard constructed a monoplane at Morris Park patterned after those built by Bleriot and Antoinette.  Completed on May 31, 1909, it was reported to be the first monoplane flown in the United States.  Beach claimed it was faster than either the Wright or Curtiss airplanes, and just as stable.  He intended to show it at the Hudson-Fulton Celebration, and fly it from New York to Albany.
The aeroplane had a 50 horsepower (37 kW) four-cylinder water cooled engine and a wing loading of 2-1/2 lbs per square foot.  The engine ran at 1000 RPM, driving a nine foot propeller at 500 RPM via a chain via a 2:1 reduction sprocket.  During early testing, the propeller turning at 300 RPM developed 325 pounds (147 kg) of thrust.  A July 1909 report in Aeronautics gives a wingspan of 38 ft (11.6 m) and a weight of 750 pounds (340 kg) including the pilot. A newspaper report in October, however, said it had a 41 ft (12.5 m) wingspan, weighed 1,100 pounds (500 kg) without the pilot, and was equipped with inflatable pontoons for water landings.


=== Henry Walden ===
In July 1908, 24-year-old Henry W. Walden, a New York City dentist and aviation enthusiast, read about the Aeronautics Society.  He joined in September of that year and began designing and building aeroplanes at Morris Park, despite a lack of training in aerodynamics.  His first design, a tandem biplane called the Walden I, was predicated on his belief that earlier designs lacked sufficient wing area.  Ready for flight testing in early spring 1909, it used an automobile engine supplied to him by the Society.  The 15 horsepower (11 kW) 500 lb (230 kg) engine proved unsuitable and he abandoned the design.  His second effort, the Walden II, was completed in late May.  This also failed to get off the ground.  Walden attributed the failure to insufficient wing area and extended the wingsan by 2 feet (0.61 m) on each side, but it was destroyed in a windstorm before another attempt at flight could be undertaken.
Encouraged by watching Glenn Curtiss's flights at the June 1909 exhibition, Walden began work on the Walden III, which he decided needed to be smaller and less complicated than his previous two.  He designed a monoplane, purchasing a three cylinder Anzani engine capable of producing 25–30 horsepower (19–22 kW).  The wing was designed in a way which made it possible to add additional panels to increase the wing area if needed.  To expedite construction, Walden hired two assistants to work on the plane, and another dentist to take over most of his practice.  The plane was completed in late November, but by that time the Society's lease was running out and the plane was moved to another field in Mineola, Long Island, where it was first test-flown on December 9.


=== American Eagle ===

In February 1908, aviator Joel T. Rice (with financial backing from John Andrew Riggs) formed the Hot Springs Airship Company in Hot Springs, Arkansas whereupon they started work on a dirigible, over 50-foot (15 m) long, named The Arkansas Traveler.   In 1909, they moved the ship to New York, where they showed it at the Hudson–Fulton Celebration.  They also began work at Morris Park on a larger ship, The American Eagle, costing over $5,000 (equivalent to $120,000 in 2024).  At the time, this was the largest steel-framed airship in the country.  The name was unpopular with New Yorkers, leading to the newspapers of the time referring to it as The Arkansas Traveler, the same name as the previous ship.  Plans were being made for the Seeing New York company to use the ship for sightseeing tours over New York City.  
The American Eagle had a 100-foot (30 m) envelope holding 33,000 cubic feet (930 m3) of gas with an 80-foot (24 m) compartment providing seating for 15 passengers.  Instead of the usual rudder, she had a large propeller mounted so that in addition to providing propulsive thrust, it could pivot left and right providing lateral control, Two smaller propellers could be pivoted up and down for vertical control, a system which Rice had patented in 1904.  The ship included a system which captured and reused hydrogen gas that leaked from the envelope.
The ship was intended to be used for cross-country flights, with the initial trip scheduled from New York to Washington DC.  Stops along the way were planned at 50–75-mile (80–121 km) intervals to show off the ship.  Riggs said that the trip was intended "to demonstrate the practical uses of a properly equipped dirigible balloon for long-continued cross-country travel".  Unfortunately, the flight never happened.  Immediately after being launched, the horizontal planes accidentally hit the propellers, destroying them, making it impossible to control the ship.  A gale-force storm two days later caused irreparable damage to the gas envelope.


== Post-aerodrome era ==

Morris Park proved to be too small to serve the needs of the Aeronautical Society.  After surveying the available locations near New York City, Glenn Curtiss recommended moving to the Hempstead Plains Aerodrome (later renamed Roosevelt Field), near Mineola, Long Island.  On May 9 (another source says April 10) 1910, a wind-blown fire destroyed the Morris Park property.  The Van Nest Hose Company responded, stopping trains on the New Haven Railroad for several hours because they needed to lay their hoses across the rails.  Despite their efforts, the fire burned all afternoon consuming the race track and several nearby buildings.  The property was later subdivided into building lots.
In the 1920s, there were efforts to create a new airport about 2 miles (3.2 km) to the northeast, in a marshy area near the Hutchinson River, which was later the site of Freedomland U.S.A. and, still later, of Co-op City. Bronx Chamber of Commerce president Logan Billingsley made one failed attempt in 1927. Another attempt in 1929 by Curtiss-Wright also failed.

About 40 motorcyclists were using the track to prepare for a race scheduled to be held on exhibition day; Thomas believed they had already cleared the track and entered the course, running at high speed.  He sustained severe injuries which were initially thought to have been fatal, but after several minutes of unconsciousness, he opened his eyes, asked for a cigarette, and refused to be taken to a hospital.  Recuperating at home, Thomas asked that the machine be repaired so another driver could use it during the exhibition.


== Retrospective ==
Two weeks after the 1908 exhibition, Lee Burridge spoke at the November 2 annual meeting of the Aero Club, reflecting on the scism which led to the founding of the Aeronautical Society.  He complained of the "apathy of the Aero Club" when, after he had identified Morris Park as a potential site, they failed to act on the opportunity.  Augustus Post, secretary of the Aero Club, replied that doing so would have split the membership into two classes, to which he was opposed.  Post added that the club was still seeking to "secure extensive grounds for motor ballooning and aeroplaning, with hydrogen gas facilities, machine shops, and suitable buildings for storage, within easy distance of the city".
Members of the opposition group who had split off to form the new society acknowledged that while Morris Park was too small, it would serve a temporary function while they continued to search for a larger facility.  A motion authorizing the Aero Club to work together with the Aeronautical Society to jointly search for a location was discussed, but failed.  


== 1909 exhibition ==

A second annual exhibition was held on June 26, 1909, with 2000 people in attendance on a day with ideal flying weather but with near-record high temperatures.  The low attendance left the Society with a $5,000 (equivalent to $120,000 in 2024) deficit.


=== Glenn Curtiss ===
The highlight of the event was a series of flights by Curtiss in a biplane named the Golden Flyer which the Society had purchased from Curtiss and his partner Augustus Herring for $5,000.  This set a number of records; the flights themselves were the first airplane flights ever taken over New York City, the purchase was the first to a civilian owner, and the Herring-Curtiss Company was the first aeroplane manufacturing company in the country.  The terms of the sale included training for two pilots (Charles Willard and Alexander Williams), and an obligation for Curtiss to fly it the exhibition.  The Curtiss design used ailerons for roll control instead of the wing warping system employed by the Wright Brothers, making the airplane more stable and more maneuverable.

The flight of the Golden Flyer created legal controversy when two months later the Wright Brothers filed a patent infringement suit against the Aeronautic Society in the United States Circuit Court, claiming infringement of their 1906 patent.   The suit (one of many the Wrights would eventually file against competitors) demanded that the Society be permanently injuncted from further infringement, disclose how much money had been made from the exhibitions, and turn over for destruction all "machinery, flying machines, and parts thereof" which infringed the patents.
The first flight was a straight-line flight covering 300 yards (270 m), averaging 30 feet (9.1 m) in altitude.  The Brooklyn Eagle noted that "his adjustment of his controls to uneven wind currents was absolutely accurate".  The remainder of the flights took place after twilight, having been delayed by puffy winds, with the event being forced to conclude as darkness fell. The rough ground at the field was a complicating factor, making landings difficult.  One flight lasted 1 minute 45 2/5 seconds, completing a lap around the 1-mile (1.6 km) track at an altitude of 20 feet (6.1 m), flying between trees along the backstretch and sometimes reaching as high as 60 feet (18 m).  The aircraft was reported as "always under perfect control".  This flight was the first time Curtiss had completed a flight around a circular course, although Henri Farman and the Wright Brothers had both already accomplished this feat.  Curtiss had hesitated before making the turn at the north end of the track, which had been criticized as being too confining.


=== William Martin ===

William H. Martin flew a glider towed by an automobile driven by his wife.  He had only gone about 50 yards (46 m) when the tow rope broke and the glider crashed; he suffered minor injuries but the aircraft was severely damaged. The safety of the craft was demonstrated on September 21 when Martin's eight-year-old granddaughter, Blanche, made several solo flights, becoming the youngest person to make a flight in a heavier-than-air craft.
Martin's glider had originally been constructed on his farm in Canton, Ohio, equipped with sled runners for operation on snow.  The V-shaped lower wings added stability as a result of the dihedral effect.  It first flew on January 12, 1909, launched from the top of a hill and towed by Martin's horse named Old Billy.  The first flight covered 200 feet (61 m) reaching a maximum altitude of 25 feet (7.6 m).  Over the next few days, over 100 flights were conducted, with Martin's wife, son, and pet dog all taking turns.  Martin brought the glider to Morris Park in May 1909, where it continued to make demonstration flights, being pulled around the track at 30 miles per hour (48 km/h) behind an automobile with a 150 ft (46 m) tow rope, and reaching altitudes as high as 75 feet (23 m).  By this time, the snow runners had been replaced with wheels.
The UK-based Flight Magazine called the Martin glider demonstration the most notable event of the day, after Curtiss's flight.  They took a negative view, however, of Martin's craft, calling it an "example of the foolhardiness of tests of this character" and writing that "there is little or nothing to be learned through being towed behind a car in this manner ... the conditions do not represent the problems of flight in the least".  They described the flight as a "short and erratic aerial journey".  They noted that the presence of the tow rope restricted operation the aircraft and negatively affected its stability.


=== Additional exhibits ===
Frederick Schneider demonstrated a motor-driven catapult-assisted airplane of his own construction, named The Brooklyn.  The craft failed to get off the ground due to a rusty launching rail and too little weight loaded into the catapult, only managing to slide along the grass for 100 feet (30 m).  There were also parachute jumps from hot air balloons, with Paul Bloomfield jumping from 1,000 feet (300 m), and Mary Hunter from an altitude reported only as "far higher" than Bloomfield's.  One of the less serious events was a "balloonatic race".  This consisted of a person attempting to run while being supported by a lighter-than-air balloon with just enough buoyancy to support the person's weight.


== The Fledglings ==

In attendance at the 1908 exhibition was painter Rudolph Dirks, better known as the cartoonist who drew The Katzenjammer Kids. Based on his experiences at the show, Dirks created an oil-on-linen painting titled The Fledglings. After the show, Dirks quickly returned to his studio in Manhattan where he began work on the painting, working from some rough pencil sketches he had made at the show.  Not having any prepared canvas on hand and wishing to begin work quickly so as not to let his memories of the event fade, Dirks repurposed a linen window shade to use as a canvas.
The painting is considered by aviation historian Tom Crouch to be "the earliest serious artistic reaction to the dawn of the air age".  It was donated by Dirks' son to the National Air and Space Museum where, as of 2025, it is on display in the Early Flight exhibit.


== Other activities ==

The March 1909 issue of Aeronautics included a paper by R. W. Jamieson describing a device used to lay out a screw propeller for an airplane, taking into account the diameter and pitch.  Jamieson described the layout process in a talk to the Society; the device itself was presented to the Society and installed at the Morris Park Aerodrome for use by the society's members.

A report in the April 1909 issue of Aeronautics described new aircraft (referred to as "machines") that were being planned or under construction by at least twenty members of the Society and would be exhibited at Morris Park in the spring of that year. The report noted that Anna Held christened the first aeroplane constructed entirely at Morris Park. The magazine had previously observed that Americans often named their aircraft, contrary to the European habit of numbering them: "Flying machines have a something that is akin to a personality, and giving them names, even if it does not help us to realize their individuality, and perhaps it may, at least it helps in a curiously subtle way to popularize them."  


=== Wilbur Kimball ===
Wilbur R. Kimball's design was a 42-foot (13 m) wingspan biplane with eight four-bladed low-pitch propellers on ball-bearing mounts driven by a 50 horsepower (37 kW) four cylinder two-stroke engine.  Lateral control was achieved by the use of the Neale system: four movable panels set vertically between the two wings. In addition to this airplane, Kimball was also working on another design for William H. Butler which would utilize a 100 horsepower (75 kW) engine.  Kimball's airplane was christened on March 14 by Anna Held as the N. Y. No. 1; the ceremony was believed to be the first time a aeroplane had ever been christened.
On December 4, 1909, a shed containing four of Kimball's aeroplanes was destroyed by fire.  The value of the aeroplanes was estimated at $25,000 (equivalent to $620,000 in 2024).


=== Frederick Schneider ===
In December 1908, a new airplane arrived at Morris Park: a biplane under construction by Frederick Schneider, who had begun construction at his home in Brooklyn, disassembled it there, delivered it to Morris Park on Christmas day, and had it reassembled by the 29th of December. The plane had a 30-foot (9.1 m) wingspan and with a pilot aboard weighed 630 pounds (290 kg) with a main wing loading of 1.7 pounds per square foot (8.3 kg/m2). A 36 horsepower (27 kW) five-cylinder air-cooled engine drove three adjustable-pitch propellers.


=== Stanley Beach and Charles Willard ===

Stanley Beach and Charles Willard constructed a monoplane at Morris Park patterned after those built by Bleriot and Antoinette.  Completed on May 31, 1909, it was reported to be the first monoplane flown in the United States.  Beach claimed it was faster than either the Wright or Curtiss airplanes, and just as stable.  He intended to show it at the Hudson-Fulton Celebration, and fly it from New York to Albany.
The aeroplane had a 50 horsepower (37 kW) four-cylinder water cooled engine and a wing loading of 2-1/2 lbs per square foot.  The engine ran at 1000 RPM, driving a nine foot propeller at 500 RPM via a chain via a 2:1 reduction sprocket.  During early testing, the propeller turning at 300 RPM developed 325 pounds (147 kg) of thrust.  A July 1909 report in Aeronautics gives a wingspan of 38 ft (11.6 m) and a weight of 750 pounds (340 kg) including the pilot. A newspaper report in October, however, said it had a 41 ft (12.5 m) wingspan, weighed 1,100 pounds (500 kg) without the pilot, and was equipped with inflatable pontoons for water landings.


=== Henry Walden ===
In July 1908, 24-year-old Henry W. Walden, a New York City dentist and aviation enthusiast, read about the Aeronautics Society.  He joined in September of that year and began designing and building aeroplanes at Morris Park, despite a lack of training in aerodynamics.  His first design, a tandem biplane called the Walden I, was predicated on his belief that earlier designs lacked sufficient wing area.  Ready for flight testing in early spring 1909, it used an automobile engine supplied to him by the Society.  The 15 horsepower (11 kW) 500 lb (230 kg) engine proved unsuitable and he abandoned the design.  His second effort, the Walden II, was completed in late May.  This also failed to get off the ground.  Walden attributed the failure to insufficient wing area and extended the wingsan by 2 feet (0.61 m) on each side, but it was destroyed in a windstorm before another attempt at flight could be undertaken.
Encouraged by watching Glenn Curtiss's flights at the June 1909 exhibition, Walden began work on the Walden III, which he decided needed to be smaller and less complicated than his previous two.  He designed a monoplane, purchasing a three cylinder Anzani engine capable of producing 25–30 horsepower (19–22 kW).  The wing was designed in a way which made it possible to add additional panels to increase the wing area if needed.  To expedite construction, Walden hired two assistants to work on the plane, and another dentist to take over most of his practice.  The plane was completed in late November, but by that time the Society's lease was running out and the plane was moved to another field in Mineola, Long Island, where it was first test-flown on December 9.


=== American Eagle ===

In February 1908, aviator Joel T. Rice (with financial backing from John Andrew Riggs) formed the Hot Springs Airship Company in Hot Springs, Arkansas whereupon they started work on a dirigible, over 50-foot (15 m) long, named The Arkansas Traveler.   In 1909, they moved the ship to New York, where they showed it at the Hudson–Fulton Celebration.  They also began work at Morris Park on a larger ship, The American Eagle, costing over $5,000 (equivalent to $120,000 in 2024).  At the time, this was the largest steel-framed airship in the country.  The name was unpopular with New Yorkers, leading to the newspapers of the time referring to it as The Arkansas Traveler, the same name as the previous ship.  Plans were being made for the Seeing New York company to use the ship for sightseeing tours over New York City.  
The American Eagle had a 100-foot (30 m) envelope holding 33,000 cubic feet (930 m3) of gas with an 80-foot (24 m) compartment providing seating for 15 passengers.  Instead of the usual rudder, she had a large propeller mounted so that in addition to providing propulsive thrust, it could pivot left and right providing lateral control, Two smaller propellers could be pivoted up and down for vertical control, a system which Rice had patented in 1904.  The ship included a system which captured and reused hydrogen gas that leaked from the envelope.
The ship was intended to be used for cross-country flights, with the initial trip scheduled from New York to Washington DC.  Stops along the way were planned at 50–75-mile (80–121 km) intervals to show off the ship.  Riggs said that the trip was intended "to demonstrate the practical uses of a properly equipped dirigible balloon for long-continued cross-country travel".  Unfortunately, the flight never happened.  Immediately after being launched, the horizontal planes accidentally hit the propellers, destroying them, making it impossible to control the ship.  A gale-force storm two days later caused irreparable damage to the gas envelope.


== Post-aerodrome era ==

Morris Park proved to be too small to serve the needs of the Aeronautical Society.  After surveying the available locations near New York City, Glenn Curtiss recommended moving to the Hempstead Plains Aerodrome (later renamed Roosevelt Field), near Mineola, Long Island.  On May 9 (another source says April 10) 1910, a wind-blown fire destroyed the Morris Park property.  The Van Nest Hose Company responded, stopping trains on the New Haven Railroad for several hours because they needed to lay their hoses across the rails.  Despite their efforts, the fire burned all afternoon consuming the race track and several nearby buildings.  The property was later subdivided into building lots.
In the 1920s, there were efforts to create a new airport about 2 miles (3.2 km) to the northeast, in a marshy area near the Hutchinson River, which was later the site of Freedomland U.S.A. and, still later, of Co-op City. Bronx Chamber of Commerce president Logan Billingsley made one failed attempt in 1927. Another attempt in 1929 by Curtiss-Wright also failed.

The '''Morris Park Aerodrome''' was a short-lived [[airfield]] in what is now the [[Morris Park, Bronx|Morris Park]] section of [[the Bronx]], New York, United States. The [[aerodrome]], which was in operation from 1908 to 1909, was the first flying field in the United States, occupying the grounds of the former [[Morris Park Racecourse]].  The newly formed [[Aeronautical Society of New York]] leased the land in 1908 and used it as an aerodrome for two years until it was developed for residential use.

The Society used the grounds for building and testing aircraft, and for putting on public exhibitions including two major events in November 1908, and June 1909.  The highlight of the former was several glider flights by sixteen-year-old [[Laurence J. Lesh|Laurence Lesh]], culminating in a crash in which he was severely injured.  The latter had flights by [[Glenn Curtiss]] in his ''[[Curtiss No. 1|Golden Flyer]]'' motorized biplane, including the first demonstration of a stable flight around a closed course using [[Aileron|ailerons]] for lateral control.  The exhibitions also featured [[Balloon (aeronautics)|balloons]], [[Kite|kites]], [[Helicopter|helicopters]], parachute jumps, and ground vehicles driven by propellers known as wind wagons.  

The aerodrome ceased operations at the end of 1909, when the land was given over to residential development.  The Society moved its operations to a larger facility on [[Long Island]], which would eventually become known as [[Roosevelt Field (airport)|Roosevelt Field]].  

== Origins ==
{{Quote box
| quote = "What the Society needed in the way of ground was not very easy to find.  Free, open space over which to fly was not alone sufficient. It was
equally, if not, indeed, still more necessary, that the grounds should be close to the city. For it was the ambition of the Society to have its
grounds so near at hand that the distance should place no obstacle in
the way even of the poorest inventor who wanted to run out to the
workshops and devote his spare hours to the material realization of his
ideas."
| author = Edward T. Tandy
| source = An Epitome of the Work of The Aeronautic Society from July, 1908, to December, 1909
| align = right
| width = 25em
| bgcolor = powderblue
| style = padding:1.5em
}}

In 1905, the [[Aero Club of America]], patterned after the [[Aéro-Club de France|Aero Club of France]], was formed as an outshoot of the [[Automobile Club of America]],<ref>{{Cite news |last=Heitman |first=Charles |date=January 2, 1910 |title=Growth of Aviation Due to Aero Club |url=https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1910/01/02/105072527.html |access-date=2025-11-04 |work=[[The New York Times]] |page=6 (Part Seven, Automobile Section) |language=en}}</ref>  Three years later, in response to sentiment that the aero club should be more active, president [[Cortlandt F. Bishop|Cortlandt Field Bishop]] appointed a Committee of Aviation, chaired by [[Albert C. Triaca|Albert Triaca]], to promote more work on aeroplanes.<ref name="The New York Times 1908b" />  The Committee, however, was unable to make any progress; Society chronicler Edward T. Tandy later wrote, "they found their efforts smothered by a cold, wet blanket of official objection. When they attempted to persevere, they were promptly stopped. The power that ruled that organization did not believe in aviation ... The doing of anything practical was not to be attempted."<ref name=":17" />{{Reference page|pages=7-8}}

Unsatisfied with the progress being made by the committee, fifty members of the club split off on June 10, 1908, forming the [[Aeronautical Society of New York]].  Initial membership included Lee Burridge, Albert Triaca, [[Wilbur Ravel Kimball|Willard Kimball]], Roger Whitman, [[William Joseph Hammer|William Hammer]], [[Albert Leo Stevens|Leo Stevens]], Daniel Brine, and [[Stanley Yale Beach|Stanley Beach]].<ref name="The New York Times 1908b">{{Cite news |date=June 11, 1908 |title=New Aeronautical Society |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1908/06/11/archives/new-aeronautical-society-organization-to-stimulate-more-activity-in.html?searchResultPosition=1 |access-date=July 29, 2025 |work=[[The New York Times]] |page=8 |language=en}}</ref>  Burridge (who would later be President of the Society<ref>{{Cite journal |date=March 13, 1909 |title=Aeronautical Notes |journal=[[Scientific American]] |volume=100 |issue=11 |page=203 |doi=10.1038/scientificamerican03131909-203 |jstor=26034548}}</ref>) spoke of plans to acquire an airfield: "this society is going to stand for something tangible, practical, and it proposes to secure experimental grounds as soon as possible where men who have been working on problems of aeronautics will be enabled to try out their machines".<ref name="The New York Times 1908b" />
That summer, the Society looked at several properties from [[New Jersey]] to [[Long Island]] and ultimately identified the grounds of the old [[Morris Park Racecourse]] as the best location.<ref name=":8">{{Cite news |date=1908-08-31 |title=Place to Test Airships |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/new-york-tribune-place-to-test-airships/184333143/ |access-date=2025-11-04 |work=[[New-York Tribune]] |page=3}}</ref> The racecourse had closed in 1904, after which the {{convert|372|acre|adj=on}} property was used for [[Auto racing|automobile]] and [[motorcycle racing]] for a few years. It was convenient to the recently opened [[West Farms Square–East Tremont Avenue station|West Farms Square subway station]] and a trolley stop, as well as a range of cafes and residences which could be had for inexpensive rents.  Proximity to public transportation was considered essential, making the field accessible to all experimenters, not just the affluent.<ref name="Crouch 2011">{{Cite journal |last=Crouch |first=Tom D. |date=Fall 2011 |title=The Aeronautic Society of New York and the Birth of American Aviation, 1908—1918 |journal=[[New York History]] |volume=92 |issue=4 |pages=268–289 |jstor=23645508}}</ref>{{Reference page|pages=273-274}}[[File:Woodmansten Inn Postcard (front).webp|thumb|The Woodmansten Inn|alt=Color picture postcard showing a three-story building in a wooded setting.  Printed under the photo is "Woodmansten Inn, Pelham Parkway and Williamsbridge Road, Westchester, N.Y."]]
The location provided open spaces on a level elevation, several existing buildings which could be repurposed as workshops, and a larger building with a neatly trimmed lawn and flower beds to use as a clubhouse.<ref name=":9">{{Cite journal |last= |last2= |date=August 1909 |title=Aeronautics |url=https://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/000495912 |journal=Aeronautics |volume=5 |issue=2 |at=Unnumbered advertisement sheet before title page |via=[[HathiTrust]]}}</ref>  The nearby Woodmansten Inn, built in 1902, had a restaurant and sleeping facilities.<ref name=":13" />  An advertisement in the 1908 exhibition program offered dinner with wine for $3.00 ({{Inflation|index=US-GDP|value=3|start_year=1908|r=0|fmt=eq}})<ref name=":18">{{Cite web |date=November 3, 1908 |title=1908 Aeronautic Society Exhibition and Tournament and Championship Motorcycle Races Program |url=https://sova.si.edu/record/nasm.xxxx.0956 |access-date=2025-11-24 |website=Smithsonian Institution Online Virtual Archives}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=4}} and Tandy described it as "one of the best and most fashionable hotels of the city".<ref name=":17" />{{Reference page|page=9}}

Morris Park Aerodrome (occasionally called the Morris Park Volery<ref name="Aeronautics 1909a">{{Cite journal |date=March 1909 |title=At Morris Park: The Aeronautic Society Buys Curtiss Flyer |url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=uiug.30112004243124&seq=80 |journal=Aeronautics |volume=4 |issue=3 |pages=104–107 |via=[[HathiTrust]]}}</ref>) was made available to members for the first time on the weekend of August 29 and 30, 1908.<ref name="Crouch 2011" />{{Reference page|page=274}}  A lease was signed on or about August 31,<ref name=":8" /> running until December 31, 1909,<ref name=":3">{{Cite news |date=September 7, 1908 |title=Plan Airship Exhibition |url=https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1908/09/07/issue.html |access-date=2025-10-28 |work=[[The New York Times]] |page=11 |language=en}}</ref> although it was already known that the land was eventually destined for residential development.<ref name=":17" />{{Reference page|page=9}}  By September, plans were being made for an exhibition where "Freak machines will have a chance to show what they can do as well as the more orthodox types."  Fences adjacent to the track were removed to provide a clear straight path of at least {{Convert|0.62|mi}}, and a machine shop was being constructed.<ref name=":3" />

== The field ==
[[File:The American turf- an historical account of racing in the United States - with biographical sketches of turf celebrities. 1898 (1898) (17975359990).jpg|thumb|Morris Park Clubhouse in 1898|alt=Photograph of an ornate five-story building with multiple setbacks, balconies, and awnings.]]
Morris Park was the first flying field in the United States<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/100958691 |title=Fifty years of powered flight, 1903-1953 |publisher=The Admaster Creations Company |year=1952 |location=Toledo, Ohio |page=59 |chapter=June 26, 1909}}</ref> although by the end of 1909, ''[[Janes All the World's Aircraft|All the World's Air-Ships]]'' by [[Fred T. Jane|Fred Jane]] listed it as one of eight such facilities in the country.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Jane |first=Fred T. |author-link=Fred T. Jane |date=1909 |title=United States |url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=mdp.39015018608466&seq=267&q1=morris |journal=All the World's Air-Ships |location=London |publisher=Sampson Low, Marston & Co. |page=252 |via=[[HathiTrust]]]}}</ref>  In addition to being used for flight instruction (being home to the International School of Aeronautics run by Albert Triaca<ref name=":9" />) the primary purpose of the field and the Society was the construction of aircraft.  Within the first 12 months of operation, 24 full-sized heavier-than-air airplanes were constructed on the field, plus an assortment of gliders, airships, and a large number of scale models. Almost 25% of the Society membership held aircraft patents or were directly involved in the construction of aircraft at the field.<ref name=":17">{{Cite book |last=Tandy |first=Edward T. |url=https://transcription.si.edu/project/12997 |title=An Epitome of the Work of The Aeronautic Society from July, 1908, to December, 1909 |publisher=The Aeronautic Society |year=c. 1910 |edition=Reprinted November, 1958 |type=}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=6}}

Lacking any hill high enough to launch a glider from, the Society built two facilities for assisting in glider launches.  The first was a catapult.  The second was a larger structure of wooden construction, which was erected without first obtaining a building permit.  After a glider spent an entire day atop the structure waiting for winds favorable for launching, city officials declared that the structure was a residence, and since it lacked both plumbing and a fire escape, condemned it, compelling it to be torn down.<ref name=":17" />{{Reference page|page=14}}

Many of the aircraft built at Morris Park were failures.  Aviation historian Paul Glenshaw wrote of the Aeronautic Society's efforts:<ref>{{Cite web |last=Glenshaw |first=Paul |date=March 2012 |title=Or Die Trying |url=https://www.smithsonianmag.com/air-space-magazine/or-die-trying-21230348/ |access-date=2025-12-08 |website=Smithsonian Magazine |language=en}}</ref>

{{Blockquote|text=The group could boast of few successes. Descriptions of the members’ experiments included words like “tree” and “fence,” coupled with “plunged” and “smashed.”}}

== 1908 exhibition ==
On October 18, the first exhibition of the Society was announced for November 3 to coincide with [[1908 United States presidential election|election day]].  There were plans for two airplanes from the [[Aerial Experiment Association]] ''([[AEA June Bug|June Bug]]'' and ''[[AEA Silver Dart|Silver Dart)]]'' to compete, a five-mile [[Airship|dirigible]] race, [[kite]]s, and [[Glider (aircraft)|gliders]]; the kite contest was open to [[Primary school|public school]] students with no entry fee.<ref name="The New York Times 1908c" /> There were also plans for one-, five-, and ten-mile [[motorcycle]] races sponsored by the [[American Motorcyclist Association|Federation of American Motorcyclists]]<ref name="Crouch 2011" />{{Reference page|page=269}} and for the [[National Weather Service|U.S. Weather Bureau]] to demonstrate the use of kites and captive balloons to collect atmospheric data.<ref name="Crouch 2011" />{{Reference page|page=277}}  [[E. Lilian Todd|Lillian Todd]], the only female member of the Society, was expected to show a "large model airplane" of her own design.<ref>{{Cite news |date=1908-11-01 |title=MIss Todd Builds Aeroplane and Teaches Boys Aeronautics |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-pittsburgh-post-miss-todd-builds-aer/185583342/ |access-date=2025-11-24 |work=[[The Pittsburgh Post]] |pages=30}}</ref><ref name=":18" />{{Reference page|page=11}}

Admission to the exhibition was $0.50 ({{Inflation|index=US|value=0.50|start_year=1908|r=2|fmt=eq}}), with the [[New York City Subway|subway]] ride from [[Manhattan]] taking 40 minutes.<ref name="Crouch 2011" />{{Reference page|page=269}}   An estimated 20,000 spectators showed up, far exceeding expectations. Although several hundred people had volunteered to act as marshals (equipped with badges and sticks), a large number of people swarmed past the gate with only about 3,500 people having paid their admission fee.<ref name="Crouch 2011" />{{Reference page|page=279}}  Tandy wrote that in the years since the race track had been in use, the fences had deteriorated and that "The payment for admission proved a matter of almost Quixotic courtesy."<ref name=":17" />{{Reference page|page=15}}

=== Laurence Lesh ===
[[File:Lawrence J. Lesh in Glider Flight at Morris Park.png|left|thumb|Lesh in the air at the 1908 exhibition|alt=A man hangs below a glider in flight.  Many people (at least 100) are watching.]]
A glider piloted by sixteen-year-old [[Laurence J. Lesh]] crashed during its third flight after reaching a maximum altitude of {{Convert|70|ft}} and travelling a total of about {{Convert|200|ft}}.<ref name="The New York Times 1908a">{{Cite news |date=November 4, 1908 |title=Man-Bird Falls and Breaks Ankle |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1908/11/04/archives/manbird-falls-and-breaks-ankle-laurence-j-lesh-comes-to-grief-at.html?searchResultPosition=1 |access-date=July 27, 2025 |work=[[The New York Times]] |page=9 |language=en}}</ref>  One account attributed the cause of the crash to inexperience flying this model of glider which lacked the rudder used on his earlier designs.<ref name=":10">{{Cite journal |date=November 14, 1908 |title=The Aeronautic Society's First Exhibition |journal=[[Scientific American]] |volume=99 |issue=20 |pages=336–338 |jstor=26019111}}</ref> Another blamed the crowd which got in his way while attempting to land.<ref name=":17" />{{Reference page|page=17}}  In any case, the injuries sustained in the crash sent Lesh to the hospital and he took a year of rehabilitative therapy to fully recover from his broken ankle.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Un gamin dans le ciel – Larry Lesh – The Flying Lad |url=https://www.cahs.com/larry-lesh-by-pierre-thiffault.html |access-date=2025-10-27 |website=Canadian Aviation Historical Society |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |date=July 1909 |title=Taft presents Wright medals |url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=uc1.b3099545&seq=35 |journal=Aeronautics |location=New York |publisher=Aeronautics Press |volume=5 |issue=1 |page=27 |via=[[HathiTrust]]}}</ref>

The glider had been launched by rope tow behind [[Thomas Motor Company#New York to Paris Race|a 1907 Thomas Flyer]] driven by [[Montague Roberts]], one of the drivers who had won the [[1908 New York to Paris Race]] in that car.<ref name="The New York Times 1908a" /><ref>{{Cite news |last=Garrett |first=Jerry |date=February 10, 2008 |title=New York to Paris the Hard Way |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/02/10/automobiles/10RACE.html |access-date=July 27, 2025 |work=[[The New York Times]] |language=en}}</ref> Montague had also competed in a 1907 24-hour race held at Morris Park when it was previously used for automobile racing.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Big Motor Race May be Repeated|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1907/09/09/archives/big-motor-race-may-be-repeated-contestants-in-morris-park-event.html|date=September 9, 1907|access-date=2025-12-01|language=en|work=[[The New York Times]]|page=5}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Montague Roberts posing in Thomas racecar, 24 hour race, 1907 Morris Park races|url=https://digitalcollections.detroitpubliclibrary.org/islandora/object/islandora:262511|website=Detroit Public LIbrary Digital Collections|access-date=2025-12-01|date=1907}}</ref>  Previous launch attempts that day had used a tow horse; out of six tries, only two got off the ground, reaching an altitude of about {{Convert|20|ft}}.<ref>{{Cite news |date=November 3, 1908 |title=Morris Park Aeronauts |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1908/11/03/archives/morris-park-aeronauts-aeroplane-cop-who-is-a-west-point-graduate.html?searchResultPosition=2 |access-date=July 27, 2025 |work=[[The New York Times]] |page=9 |language=en}}</ref>

Lesh had also planned to show a large [[box kite]] that day.<ref>{{Cite news |date=1908-11-01 |title=Canadian Glider in Town |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1908/11/01/archives/two-runs-to-hounds-meadow-brook-colony-has-fox-chase-and-later-a.html?searchResultPosition=1 |access-date=2025-10-27 |work=[[The New York Times]] |page=3 |language=en}}</ref>  Lesh, a protégé of [[Octave Chanute]], was a native of [[Iowa]] who moved to [[Montreal]] as a child.  He was the first known aviator in Canada, having built and flown horse-drawn gliders as early as 1907. Lesh also completed a record-setting 24 minute, {{Convert|6.2|mi|adj=on}} flight in 1907 towed by a motor boat on the [[St. Lawrence River]].<ref name=":0" />

=== Wind wagon races ===
[[File:Glenn Curtiss Seated on a Wind Wagon.png|thumb|Glenn Curtiss on a wind wagon (date and location unknown)|alt=A man wearing a white shirt, tie, and cap sits on a three-wheeled vehicle.  The wheels appear to be from a bicycle.  In the rear is some machinery and a large propeller.  The man is holding in one hand what appears to be a tiller for steering the front wheel, and in the other controls for the machinery.]]The exhibition included a wind wagon contest, these being wheeled ground vehicles driven by propeller thrust.<ref name="The New York Times 1908c">{{Cite news |date=October 18, 1908 |title=Aeronauts to Compete |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1908/10/18/archives/aeronauts-to-compete-contests-at-morris-park-for-aeroplanes.html?searchResultPosition=1 |access-date=July 27, 2025 |work=[[The New York Times]] |language=en}}</ref>  ''[[The New York Times]]'' described them as resembling "a huge tricycle with a propeller eight feet long in front and a gasoline motor behind".<ref>{{Cite news |date=1914-04-21 |title=Take Dr. J.P. Thomas on Charge of Fraud; Balloonist is Accused of Making Unwarranted Claims for His Prepared Food |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1914/04/21/archives/take-dr-jp-thomas-on-charge-of-fraud-balloonist-is-accused-of.html?searchResultPosition=2 |access-date=2025-10-27 |work=[[The New York Times]] |page=8 |language=en}}</ref>  Inventors scheduled to show their wagons included astronomer [[William Henry Pickering|William Pickering]], aviation pioneer [[Glenn Curtiss]], W. A. Custard,<ref name="The New York Times 1908c" /> and [[Julian P. Thomas]].<ref name=":19">{{Cite news |date=November 2, 1908 |title=Dr. J. P. Thomas Hurt, Wind Wagon a Wreck |url=https://www.loc.gov/resource/sn83030214/1908-11-02/ed-1/?sp=1&q=%22morris+park+aerodrome%22&r=0.24,0.355,0.628,0.515,0 |access-date=December 7, 2025 |work=[[New York Tribune]] |page=1}}</ref> According to Curtiss, the purpose of the wind wagon was to test the power of motors and the efficiency of propellers<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Curtiss |first1=Glenn H. |author-link1=Glenn Curtiss |url=https://gutenberg.org/files/66511/66511-h/66511-h.htm |title=The Curtiss Aviation Book |last2=Post |first2=Augustus |date=October 1912 |publisher=Frederick A. Stokes Company |location=New York |chapter=Part I, Chapter IV: Baldwin's Balloon |via=[[Project Gutenberg]]}}</ref> and it had no commercial value.<ref>{{Cite magazine |date=November 1906 |title=A Motor Wind Wagon |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9Xo3AQAAMAAJ&q=%22wind%20wagon%22 |access-date=October 29, 2025 |magazine=[[Popular Mechanics]] |page=1106 |volume=8 |issue=11}}</ref>

Thomas's machine was wrecked two days before the exhibition, when he crashed during a practice run while trying to avoid a motorcycle.  About 40 motorcyclists were using the track to prepare for a race scheduled to be held on exhibition day; Thomas believed they had already cleared the track and entered the course, running at high speed.  He sustained severe injuries which were initially thought to have been fatal, but after several minutes of [[unconsciousness]], he opened his eyes, asked for a [[cigarette]], and refused to be taken to a hospital.  Recuperating at home, Thomas asked that the machine be repaired so another driver could use it during the exhibition.<ref name=":19" />

== Retrospective ==
Two weeks after the 1908 exhibition, Lee Burridge spoke at the November 2 annual meeting of the Aero Club, reflecting on the scism which led to the founding of the Aeronautical Society.  He complained of the "apathy of the Aero Club" when, after he had identified Morris Park as a potential site, they failed to act on the opportunity.  [[Augustus Post]], secretary of the Aero Club, replied that doing so would have split the membership into two classes, to which he was opposed.  Post added that the club was still seeking to "secure extensive grounds for motor ballooning and aeroplaning, with hydrogen gas facilities, machine shops, and suitable buildings for storage, within easy distance of the city".<ref name=":23" />

Members of the opposition group who had split off to form the new society acknowledged that while Morris Park was too small, it would serve a temporary function while they continued to search for a larger facility.  A motion authorizing the Aero Club to work together with the Aeronautical Society to jointly search for a location was discussed, but failed.<ref name=":23">{{Cite news |date=November 15, 1908 |title=Toilers on Midair Machines |url=https://www.loc.gov/resource/sn83030272/1908-11-15/ed-1/?sp=37 |access-date=November 14, 2025 |work=[[The Sun (New York City)|The Sun]] |location=New York |page=8 (section three) |via=[[Library of Congress]]}}</ref>  

== 1909 exhibition ==
[[File:Curtiss Aeroplane in Flight 1909.png|thumb|The Golden Flyer at Morris Park, 1909|alt=A biplane in flight.  A man is visible at the controls.]]
A second annual exhibition was held on June 26, 1909, with 2000 people in attendance<ref name=":1" /> on a day with ideal flying weather<ref name=":2">{{Cite news |date=June 27, 1909 |title=Curtiss Makes Fine Flight at Morris Park Aerodrome |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/brooklyn-eagle-curtiss-makes-fine-flight/183866757/ |work=[[Brooklyn Eagle]] |page=57}}</ref> but with near-record high temperatures.<ref name=":14">{{Cite journal |date=August 1909 |title=At Morris Park: Aeroplane Flights at Aeronautic Society Exhibition |url=https://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/000495912 |journal=Aeronautics |publisher=Aeronautical Society of America |volume=5 |issue=2 |pages=53–56 |via=[[Hathi Trust]]}}</ref>  The low attendance left the Society with a $5,000 ({{Inflation|index=US-GDP|value=5000|start_year=1908|r=-4|fmt=eq}}) deficit.<ref name=":14" />

=== Glenn Curtiss ===
The highlight of the event was a series of flights by Curtiss in a [[biplane]] named the ''[[Curtiss No. 1|Golden Flyer]]'' which the Society had purchased from Curtiss and his partner [[Augustus Moore Herring|Augustus Herring]] for $5,000.<ref name=":11">{{Cite report |url=https://npshistory.com/publications/nhl/theme-studies/aviation.pdf |title=American Aviation Heritage: Identifying and Evaluating Nationally Significant Properties in U.S. Aviation History |date=March 2011 |publisher=National Park Service |page=28}}</ref>  This set a number of records; the flights themselves were the first airplane flights ever taken over New York City,<ref>{{Cite journal |date=April 1959 |title=Half a Century Ago |journal=Air Power Historian |volume=6 |issue=2 |page=137 |jstor=44513573}}</ref> the purchase was the first to a civilian owner, and the [[Curtiss Aeroplane and Motor Company|Herring-Curtiss Company]] was the first aeroplane manufacturing company in the country.<ref name=":11" />  The terms of the sale included training for two pilots (Charles Willard and Alexander Williams<ref>{{Cite web |title=Teaching the World to Fly |url=https://glennhcurtissmuseum.org/exhibits/dawn-of-a-legacy/ |access-date=2025-12-13 |website=Glenn H. Curtiss Museum |language=en-US}}</ref>), and an obligation for Curtiss to fly it the exhibition.  The Curtiss design used [[Aileron|ailerons]] for [[Aircraft flight control system|roll control]] instead of the [[wing warping]] system employed by the [[Wright brothers|Wright Brothers]], making the airplane more stable and more maneuverable.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Goldstone |first=Lawrence |title=Birdmen: The Wright Brothers, Glenn Curtiss, and the Battle to Control the Skies |publisher=[[Ballantine Books]] |year=2014 |isbn=978-0-345-53804-8 |location=New York |pages=183-184 (ebook edition) |chapter=16: The Toast of France}}</ref>

The flight of the Golden Flyer created legal controversy when two months later the Wright Brothers filed a [[Patent infringement|patent infringement suit]] against the Aeronautic Society in the [[United States circuit court|United States Circuit Court]], claiming infringement of their 1906 patent.   The suit ([[Wright brothers patent war|one of many]] the Wrights would eventually file against competitors) demanded that the Society be permanently [[Injunction|injuncted]] from further infringement, disclose how much money had been made from the exhibitions, and turn over for destruction all "machinery, flying machines, and parts thereof" which infringed the patents.<ref>{{Cite news |date=1909-08-20 |title=Wrights Bring Suit |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/new-york-tribune-wrights-bring-suit-par/184995315/ |access-date=2025-11-15 |work=[[New-York Tribune]] |pages=[https://www.newspapers.com/article/new-york-tribune-wrights-bring-suit-par/184995315/ 1] and [https://www.newspapers.com/article/new-york-tribune-wrights-bring-suit-par/184995379/ 2]}}</ref>

The first flight was a straight-line flight covering {{Convert|300|yd}}, averaging {{Convert|30|ft}} in altitude.  ''[[Brooklyn Eagle|The Brooklyn Eagle]]'' noted that "his adjustment of his controls to uneven wind currents was absolutely accurate".<ref name=":2" />  The remainder of the flights took place after twilight, having been delayed by puffy winds, with the event being forced to conclude as darkness fell. The rough ground at the field was a complicating factor, making landings difficult.<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal |last=Quiz |date=August 1909 |title=Aeronautical Society's Second Show |url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=hvd.hx3sdw&seq=50&q1=%22morris+park%22 |journal=American Aeronaut |volume=1 |issue=1 |pages=44–45 |via=[[HathiTrust]]}}</ref>  One flight lasted 1 minute 45 2/5 seconds, completing a lap around the {{Convert|1|mi|adj=on}} track at an altitude of {{Convert|20|ft|adj=off}}, flying between trees along the [[backstretch]] and sometimes reaching as high as {{Convert|60|ft|adj=off}}.  The aircraft was reported as "always under perfect control".<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" />  This flight was the first time Curtiss had completed a flight around a circular course, although [[Henri Farman]] and the Wright Brothers had both already accomplished this feat.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Voisin-Farman |url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/Voisin-Farman-I |access-date=2025-10-28 |website=[[Encyclopedia Britannica]] |language=en}}</ref>  Curtiss had hesitated before making the turn at the north end of the track, which had been criticized as being too confining.<ref name=":14" />

=== William Martin ===
[[File:William Martin Glider at Morris Park 1909.png|left|thumb|William Martin's glider at Morris Park|alt=An aircraft in flight, just barely above the ground.  It is banked at approximately 45 degrees.]]
William H. Martin flew a glider towed by an automobile driven by his wife.  He had only gone about {{Convert|50|yd}} when the tow rope broke and the glider crashed; he suffered minor injuries but the aircraft was severely damaged.<ref name=":1">{{Cite news |date=June 27, 1909 |title=Throngs Witness Flying Contests |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/oakland-tribune-throngs-witness-flying-c/183866080/ |work=[[Oakland Tribune]] |page=19}}</ref> The safety of the craft was demonstrated on September 21 when Martin's eight-year-old granddaughter, Blanche, made several solo flights, becoming the youngest person to make a flight in a heavier-than-air craft.<ref name=":4">{{Cite report |url=https://mapsairmuseum.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/Martin-Glider.pdf |title=William H. Martin Glider |date=}}</ref>

Martin's glider had originally been constructed on his farm in [[Canton, Ohio]], equipped with sled runners for operation on snow.  The V-shaped lower wings added stability as a result of the [[Dihedral (aeronautics)|dihedral effect]].  It first flew on January 12, 1909, launched from the top of a hill and towed by Martin's horse named Old Billy.  The first flight covered {{Convert|200|ft|adj=off}} reaching a maximum altitude of {{Convert|25|ft|adj=off}}.  Over the next few days, over 100 flights were conducted, with Martin's wife, son, and pet dog all taking turns.  Martin brought the glider to Morris Park in May 1909, where it continued to make demonstration flights, being pulled around the track at {{Convert|30|mph}} behind an automobile with a {{Convert|150|ft|abbr=on}} tow rope, and reaching altitudes as high as {{Convert|75|ft}}.  By this time, the snow runners had been replaced with wheels.<ref name=":4" />

The UK-based [[Flight International|Flight Magazine]] called the Martin glider demonstration the most notable event of the day, after Curtiss's flight.  They took a negative view, however, of Martin's craft, calling it an "example of the foolhardiness of tests of this character" and writing that "there is little or nothing to be learned through being towed behind a car in this manner ... the conditions do not represent the problems of flight in the least".  They described the flight as a "short and erratic aerial journey".  They noted that the presence of the tow rope restricted operation the aircraft and negatively affected its stability.<ref>{{Cite journal |date=July 17, 1909 |title=The Morris Park Meeting |url=https://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/102417939 |journal=[[Flight]] |location=London |publisher=United Service and Royal Aero Club (IPC Transport Press Ltd) |volume=1 |issue=29 |page=423 |via=[[Hathi Trust]]}}</ref>

=== Additional exhibits ===
Frederick Schneider demonstrated a motor-driven [[Aircraft catapult|catapult-assisted]] airplane of his own construction, named ''The Brooklyn''.  The craft failed to get off the ground due to a rusty launching rail and too little weight loaded into the catapult, only managing to slide along the grass for {{Convert|100|ft}}.  There were also [[parachute]] jumps from [[Hot air balloon|hot air balloons]], with Paul Bloomfield jumping from {{Convert|1000|ft|adj=off}}, and Mary Hunter from an altitude reported only as "far higher" than Bloomfield's.<ref name=":2" />  One of the less serious events was a "balloonatic race".  This consisted of a person attempting to run while being supported by a lighter-than-air balloon with just enough buoyancy to support the person's weight.<ref name=":5" />

== ''The Fledglings'' ==
[[File:Detail from "The Fledglings".jpg|thumb|Detail from ''The Fledglings''|alt=A scene of an aviation exhibition.  Several winged craft are on the ground; some have propellers, some do not.  A car appears to be pulling one of them.  Dozens of people are milling around, some with bicycles.  In the background, a boy flies a kite.]]
In attendance at the 1908 exhibition was painter [[Rudolph Dirks]], better known as the cartoonist who drew ''[[The Katzenjammer Kids]]''. Based on his experiences at the show, Dirks created an oil-on-linen painting titled ''The Fledglings.''<ref name="Crouch 2012">{{Cite web |last=Crouch |first=Tom |date=May 2012 |title=The Katzenjammer Kids Take to the Air |url=https://www.smithsonianmag.com/air-space-magazine/the-katzenjammer-kids-take-to-the-air-120519321/ |access-date=July 26, 2025 |website=[[Smithsonian Magazine]] |language=en}}</ref> After the show, Dirks quickly returned to his [[studio]] in Manhattan where he began work on the painting, working from some rough pencil sketches he had made at the show.<ref>{{Cite news |date=July 9, 1986 |title=Rudolph Dirks: Creator of Comic 'Katzenjammer Kids' was also a Talented and Serious Painter |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/morning-sentinel-rudolph-dirks-creator/184756578/ |access-date=November 11, 2025 |work=[[Morning Sentinel]] |location=Waterville, Maine |page=14}}</ref>  Not having any prepared canvas on hand and wishing to begin work quickly so as not to let his memories of the event fade, Dirks repurposed a linen window shade to use as a canvas.<ref name="Crouch 2012" />

The painting is considered by aviation historian [[Tom D. Crouch|Tom Crouch]] to be "the earliest serious artistic reaction to the dawn of the air age".<ref name="Crouch 2012" />  It was donated by Dirks' son to the [[National Air and Space Museum]] where, {{As of|2025|lc=y}}, it is on display in the Early Flight exhibit.<ref name="National Air and Space Museum 20112">{{Cite web |date=October 25, 2011 |title=Rudolph Dirks and The Fledglings |url=https://airandspace.si.edu/events/rudolph-dirks-and-fledglings |access-date=July 26, 2025 |website=[[National Air and Space Museum]] |language=en}}</ref>
