The report noted that [[Anna Held]] christened the first aeroplane constructed entirely at Morris Park.<ref>{{Cite journal |date=April 1909 |title=At Morris Park: Many Members of Aeronautic Society Building Machines |url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=uiug.30112004243124&seq=133 |journal=Aeronautics |volume=4 |issue=4 |pages=145–149 |via=[[HathiTrust]]}}</ref> The magazine had previously observed that Americans often named their aircraft, contrary to the European habit of numbering them: "Flying machines have a something that is akin to a personality, and giving them names, even if it does not help us to realize their individuality, and perhaps it may, at least it helps in a curiously subtle way to popularize them."<ref name="Aeronautics 1909a" />  [[File:Kimball aeroplane being christened at Morris Park Aerodrome, 1909.png|thumb|Anna Held christening the ''N.Y. No. 1'' at Morris Park|alt=A biplane with multiple propellers sitting on the ground.  Around it are approximately 40 men.  A woman in fancy clothes is standing in front of the plane.]]

=== Wilbur Kimball ===
[[Wilbur Ravel Kimball|Wilbur R. Kimball's]] design was a {{Convert|42|ft|adj=on}} wingspan biplane with eight four-bladed low-pitch propellers on ball-bearing mounts driven by a {{Convert|50|hp}} four cylinder [[two-stroke engine]].<ref name="Aeronautics 1909b" />  Lateral control was achieved by the use of the Neale system: four movable panels set vertically between the two wings.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gilpatric |first=John Guy |date=January 28, 1911 |title=Correspondence: Neale Control |url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=mdp.39015084425761&seq=98&q1=neale |journal=Flight |publisher=Royal Aero Club of the United Kingdom |publication-place=London |volume=4 |issue=3 |page=80 |via=[[HathiTrust]]}}</ref> In addition to this airplane, Kimball was also working on another design for William H. Butler which would utilize a {{Convert|100|hp}} engine.<ref name="Aeronautics 1909b">{{Cite journal |date=January 1909 |title=Flying Machines at the Morris Park Volery |url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=uiug.30112004243124&seq=13 |journal=Aeronautics |volume=4 |issue=1 |pages=7–9 |via=[[HathiTrust]]}}</ref>  Kimball's airplane was christened on March 14 by Anna Held as the ''N. Y. No. 1;'' the ceremony was believed to be the first time a aeroplane had ever been christened.<ref name="Aeronautics 1909a" />

On December 4, 1909, a shed containing four of Kimball's aeroplanes was destroyed by fire.  The value of the aeroplanes was estimated at $25,000 ({{Inflation|index=US-GDP|value=25000|start_year=1909|r=-4|fmt=eq}}).<ref>{{Cite news |date=1909-12-04 |title=Four Aeroplanes are Destroyed by Fire |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/ledger-star-four-aeroplanes-are-destroye/186405310/ |access-date=2025-12-07 |work=[[Ledger-Star]] |location=Norfolk |page=11 |agency=Associated Press}}</ref>

=== Frederick Schneider ===
In December 1908, a new airplane arrived at Morris Park: a biplane under construction by Frederick Schneider,{{Efn|group=note|Spelled as Shneider or Schneider in different sources.}} who had begun construction at his home in [[Brooklyn]], disassembled it there, delivered it to Morris Park on Christmas day, and had it reassembled by the 29th of December. The plane had a {{Convert|30|ft|adj=on}} wingspan and with a pilot aboard weighed {{Convert|630|lb}} with a main wing loading of {{Convert|1.7|lb/ft2}}. A {{Convert|36|hp}} five-cylinder air-cooled engine drove three adjustable-pitch propellers.<ref name="Aeronautics 1909b" />

=== Stanley Beach and Charles Willard ===
[[File:Beach-Willard Monoplane, Charles F. Willard and Stanley Yale Beach1.jpg|alt=Head-on photograph of a monoplane.  A man stands to the side of one wingtip.|thumb|Beach-Willard Monoplane]]
Stanley Beach and [[Charles F. Willard|Charles Willard]] constructed a [[monoplane]] at Morris Park patterned after those built by [[Louis Blériot|Bleriot]] and [[Antoinette (manufacturer)|Antoinette]].<ref name=":21">{{Cite journal |date=July 1909 |title=At Morris Park: The Beach-Willard Monoplane |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/American_Magazine_of_Aeronautics/wrIVAQAAIAAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1 |journal=[[Aeronautics]] |volume=5 |issue=1 |pages=13-17}}</ref>  Completed on May 31, 1909, it was reported to be the first monoplane flown in the United States.  Beach claimed it was faster than either the Wright or Curtiss airplanes, and just as stable.  He intended to show it at the Hudson-Fulton Celebration, and fly it from New York to [[Albany, New York|Albany]].<ref name=":20">{{Cite news |date=October 2, 1909 |title=Monoplane in Competition |url=https://www.loc.gov/resource/sn83045462/1909-10-02/ed-1/?sp=11&q=%22morris+park+aerodrome%22&r=0.309,-0.026,0.383,0.314,0 |work=[[The Evening Star]] |location=Washington, D.C. |page=11 (part 1)}}</ref>

The aeroplane had a {{Convert|50|hp}} four-cylinder [[Water cooling|water cooled engine]] and a [[wing loading]] of 2-1/2 lbs per square foot.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Aviators Eager for Aerial Flights. |url=https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1909/06/27/106720672.html |access-date=2025-12-07 |work=[[The New York Times]] |page=3 (Section 4: Sporting News) |language=en |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>  The engine ran at 1000 RPM, driving a nine foot propeller at 500 RPM via a [[Chain drive|chain]] via a 2:1 reduction [[sprocket]].<ref name=":20" />  During early testing, the propeller turning at 300 RPM developed {{Convert|325|lb}} of [[thrust]].<ref>{{Cite journal |date=September 1909 |title=At Morris Park: Continued Activity at Aeronautic Society Grounds |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/American_Magazine_of_Aeronautics/wrIVAQAAIAAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=%22beach-willard%22+monoplane&pg=PA98&printsec=frontcover |journal=Aeronautics |volume=5 |issue=3 |pages=97-98}}</ref>  A July 1909 report in ''Aeronautics'' gives a wingspan of {{Convert|38|ft|abbr=on|sigfig=3}} and a weight of {{Convert|750|lb|sigfig=2}} including the pilot.<ref name=":21" /> A newspaper report in October, however, said it had a {{Convert|41|ft|abbr=on|sigfig=3}} wingspan, weighed {{Convert|1100|lb|sigfig=2}} without the pilot, and was equipped with inflatable [[Float (nautical)|pontoons]] for water landings.<ref name=":20" />

=== Henry Walden ===
In July 1908, 24-year-old Henry W. Walden, a New York City dentist and aviation enthusiast, read about the Aeronautics Society.  He joined in September of that year and began designing and building aeroplanes at Morris Park, despite a lack of training in aerodynamics.  His first design, a [[tandem]] biplane called the ''Walden I'', was predicated on his belief that earlier designs lacked sufficient wing area.  Ready for flight testing in early spring 1909, it used an automobile engine supplied to him by the Society.  The {{Convert|15|hp}} {{Convert|500|lb|sigfig=2|abbr=on}} engine proved unsuitable and he abandoned the design.  His second effort, the ''Walden II'', was completed in late May.  This also failed to get off the ground.  Walden attributed the failure to insufficient wing area and extended the wingsan by {{Convert|2|ft}} on each side, but it was destroyed in a windstorm before another attempt at flight could be undertaken.<ref name=":22">{{Cite web |title=Walden, Henry W. |url=https://sova.si.edu/record/nasm.xxxx.0450/ref339?q=henry+walden |access-date=2025-12-09 |website=National Air and Space Museum Archives: Harold E. Morehouse Flying Pioneers Biographies Collection}}</ref>

Encouraged by watching Glenn Curtiss's flights at the June 1909 exhibition, Walden began work on the ''Walden III,'' which he decided needed to be smaller and less complicated than his previous two.  He designed a monoplane, purchasing a [[Anzani 3-cylinder fan engines|three cylinder Anzani engine]] capable of producing {{Convert|25-30|hp}}.  The wing was designed in a way which made it possible to add additional panels to increase the wing area if needed.  To expedite construction, Walden hired two assistants to work on the plane, and another dentist to take over most of his practice.  The plane was completed in late November, but by that time the Society's lease was running out and the plane was moved to [[Roosevelt Field (airport)|another field in Mineola, Long Island,]] where it was first test-flown on December 9.<ref name=":22" />

=== American Eagle ===
[[File:Riggs-Rice airship American Eagle, Morris Park Aerodrome, 1909.jpg|thumb|American Eagle at Morris Park, 1909|left|alt=A dirigible in flight.  A long truss-like structure with three propellers at one end is slung beneath the gas balloon by a system of ropes.  Two men, dwarfed by the size of the balloon, are inside the truss.  A bunch of men are on the ground, near the truss.]]
In February 1908, aviator [[Joel T. Rice]] (with financial backing from [[John Andrew Riggs]]<ref name=":6">{{Cite web |title=John Andrew Riggs (1867–1936) |url=https://encyclopediaofarkansas.net/entries/john-andrew-riggs-5509/ |access-date=2025-11-03 |website=Encyclopedia of Arkansas |language=en-US}}</ref>) formed the [[Hot Springs Airship Company]] in [[Hot Springs, Arkansas]] whereupon they started work on a [[Airship|dirigible]], over {{Convert|50|ft|adj=on}} long, named ''The Arkansas Traveler.''<ref>{{Cite web |last=Rumley |first=Chris |date=June 16, 2010 |title=Arkansas Aviation History |url=https://www.littlerock.af.mil/News/Commentaries/Display/Article/358004/arkansas-aviation-history/ |website=Little Rock Air Force Base}}</ref>   In 1909, they moved the ship to New York, where they showed it at the [[Hudson–Fulton Celebration]].  They also began work at Morris Park on a larger ship, ''The American Eagle,'' costing over $5,000 ({{Inflation|index=US-GDP|value=5000|start_year=1909|r=-4|fmt=eq}}).  At the time, this was the largest steel-framed airship in the country.<ref name=":6" />  The name was unpopular with New Yorkers, leading to the newspapers of the time referring to it as ''The Arkansas Traveler'', the same name as the previous ship.<ref name=":7">{{Cite journal |last=Wade |first=Stephanie Haught |date=Autumn 2020 |title=John Andrew Riggs and Arkansas's Primary Suffrage Bill |journal=[[The Arkansas Historical Quarterly]] |volume=79 |issue=3 |page=258 |jstor=27019093}}</ref>  Plans were being made for the [[Seeing New York]] company to use the ship for sightseeing tours over New York City.<ref>{{Cite news |date=September 22, 1909 |title=A Seeing-New-York Airship |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-new-york-times-a-seeing-new-york-air/184853593/ |access-date=2025-11-13 |work=[[The New York Times]] |page=1}}</ref>  

''The American Eagle'' had a {{Convert|100|ft|adj=on}} envelope holding {{Convert|33000|cuft|adj=off}} of gas with an {{Convert|80|ft|adj=on}} compartment providing seating for 15 passengers.<ref name=":15" />  Instead of the usual rudder, she had a large propeller mounted so that in addition to providing propulsive thrust, it could [[Thrust vectoring|pivot left and right providing lateral control]], Two smaller propellers could be pivoted up and down for vertical control, a system which Rice had patented in 1904.  The ship included a system which captured and reused hydrogen gas that leaked from the envelope.<ref name=":16" />

The ship was intended to be used for cross-country flights, with the initial trip scheduled from New York to [[Washington, D.C.|Washington DC]].  Stops along the way were planned at {{Convert|50-75|mi|adj=on}} intervals to show off the ship.  Riggs said that the trip was intended "to demonstrate the practical uses of a properly equipped dirigible balloon for long-continued cross-country travel".<ref name=":16">{{Cite news |date=October 10, 1909 |title=Build Big Airshop for Southern Tour |url=https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1909/10/10/106722616.html?pageNumber=20 |access-date=November 3, 2025 |work=[[The New York Times]] |page=20}}</ref><ref name=":15">{{Cite news |date=September 22, 1909 |title=A Seeing-New-York Airship |url=https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1909/09/22/101030329.html |access-date=2025-11-03 |work=[[The New York Times]] |page=1 |language=en |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>  Unfortunately, the flight never happened.  Immediately after being launched, the horizontal planes accidentally hit the propellers, destroying them, making it impossible to control the ship.  A gale-force storm two days later caused irreparable damage to the gas envelope.<ref name=":7" />

== Post-aerodrome era ==
[[File:Auction Sale of Morris Park Race Track.pdf|thumb|Publicity booklet for Morris Park Race Track final auction.]]
Morris Park proved to be too small to serve the needs of the Aeronautical Society.  After surveying the available locations near New York City, Glenn Curtiss recommended moving to the Hempstead Plains Aerodrome (later renamed [[Roosevelt Field (airport)|Roosevelt Field]]), near [[Mineola, New York|Mineola, Long Island]].<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Curtiss |first1=Glenn H. |author-link1=Glenn Curtiss |url=https://gutenberg.org/files/66511/66511-h/66511-h.htm |title=The Curtiss Aviation Book |last2=Post |first2=Augustus |date=October 1912 |publisher=Frederick A. Stokes Company |location=New York |chapter=Part II, Chapter IV: First Flights in New York City |via=[[Project Gutenberg]]}}</ref>  On May 9 (another source says April 10<ref name=":12">{{Cite news |date=April 11, 1910 |title=Flames Sweep Old Morris Park |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1910/04/11/archives/flames-sweep-old-morris-park-track-westchester-village-endangered.html |access-date=July 27, 2025 |work=[[The New York Times]] |page=18 |language=en}}</ref>) 1910, a wind-blown fire destroyed the Morris Park property.  The [[Van Nest Hose Company]] responded, stopping trains on the [[New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad|New Haven Railroad]] for several hours because they needed to lay their hoses across the rails.  Despite their efforts, the fire burned all afternoon consuming the race track and several nearby buildings.<ref name=":13">{{Cite news |last=Lewis |first=John |date=1982-05-23 |title=Morris Park's Past Marked by Two Fires |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/daily-news-morris-parks-past-marked-by/184563472/ |access-date=2025-11-08 |work=[[New York Daily News|Daily News]] |location=New York |page=28}}</ref>  The property was later subdivided into building lots.<ref name=":12" />

In the 1920s, there were efforts to create a new airport about {{Convert|2|mi}} to the northeast, in a marshy area near the [[Hutchinson River]], which was later the site of [[Freedomland U.S.A.]] and, still later, of [[Co-op City, Bronx|Co-op City]]. Bronx Chamber of Commerce president [[Logan Billingsley]] made one failed attempt in 1927. Another attempt in 1929 by [[Curtiss-Wright]] also failed.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Stone |first=Andrea |date=August 2017 |title=Bronx Airport? Denied! |url=https://www.smithsonianmag.com/air-space-magazine/18_aug2017-oo-180963929/ |access-date=July 28, 2025 |website=[[Smithsonian Magazine]] |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Williams |first=Keith |date=September 28, 2017 |title=The Bronx Airport That Never Was |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/09/28/nyregion/the-bronx-airport-that-never-was.html |access-date=July 28, 2025 |work=[[The New York Times]] |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite report |url=https://eds.p.ebscohost.com/eds/pdfviewer/pdfviewer?vid=1&sid=071eca45-205c-48b2-9c19-3a5a897b8e17%40redis |title=Why the Bronx Never Got an Airport |last=Stone |first=Andrea |date=<!-- undated --> |publisher=Bronx Historical Society |via=[[EBSCO Information Services|Ebsco]]}}</ref>
